results.name: in_range_effect
results.description: Among sets with >=2 examples, yes-rate for targets inside [min example, max example] minus yes-rate for targets outside that range; observed above null_mean means people favour interpolation within the example span more than the model (interval-like generalization under-produced), below means the model over-weights range.
results.code:
# name: in_range_effect
# description: Among sets with >=2 examples, yes-rate for targets inside [min example, max example] minus yes-rate for targets outside that range; observed above null_mean means people favour interpolation within the example span more than the model (interval-like generalization under-produced), below means the model over-weights range.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    m = n >= 2
    inside = (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    a = m & inside; b = m & ~inside
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: last_digit_match_effect
results.description: Yes-rate for targets whose last digit equals the last digit of at least one example minus yes-rate for targets matching none; observed above null_mean means people generalize by shared final digit (even partially/for mixed sets) more than the model, below means less.

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: OLS slope of yes (rating) on trial_index, per 100 trials; the model has no time dependence, so observed slope far from null_mean means people drift toward more (positive) or fewer (negative) yeses over the session than the model predicts.

results.name: set_size_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes on the number of examples in the set (1-4); observed more negative than null_mean means people tighten generalization with more examples more than the model (stronger size-principle), less negative/positive means the model's size principle is too strong.

results.name: recency_last_vs_first
results.description: Among sets with >=2 examples, yes-rate for targets closer to the last-shown example minus yes-rate for targets closer to the first-shown example; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null_mean means a recency effect (last example weighs more) the model misses, below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first
# description: Among sets with >=2 examples, yes-rate for targets closer to the last-shown example minus yes-rate for targets closer to the first-shown example; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null_mean means a recency effect (last example weighs more) the model misses, below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = parts.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    vals = parts.values
    first = vals[:, 0]
    idx = np.clip(n - 1, 0, None)
    last = vals[np.arange(len(vals)), idx]
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    m = n >= 2
    dl = np.abs(t - last); dfi = np.abs(t - first)
    a = m & (dl < dfi); b = m & (dfi < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: cell_extremity
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells whose yes-rate is <= 0.12 or >= 0.88 (near-unanimous no or yes); observed below null_mean means the model's predictions are too all-or-none (people are more graded/uncertain), above means people are more categorical than the model.

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share parity, yes-rate for targets of the same parity minus yes-rate for opposite-parity targets; observed above null_mean means people generalize by parity more strongly than the model, below means the model over-relies on odd/even.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share parity, yes-rate for targets of the same parity minus yes-rate for opposite-parity targets; observed above null_mean means people generalize by parity more strongly than the model, below means the model over-relies on odd/even.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, np.mod(ex, 2))
    allodd = np.nansum(par == 1, axis=1) == n
    alleven = np.nansum(par == 0, axis=1) == n
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    m = (n >= 2) & (allodd | alleven)
    setpar = np.where(allodd, 1, 0)
    match = (t % 2) == setpar
    a = m & match; b = m & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: distance_gradient
results.description: Pearson correlation between yes and log(1 + distance from the target to the nearest example); observed more negative than null_mean means people show a stronger numeric-similarity (magnitude proximity) gradient than the model, less negative means weaker.
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient
# description: Pearson correlation between yes and log(1 + distance from the target to the nearest example); observed more negative than null_mean means people show a stronger numeric-similarity (magnitude proximity) gradient than the model, less negative means weaker.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values[:, None]
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t), axis=1)
    x = np.log1p(d)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if np.std(x) == 0 or np.std(y) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])
